title: India's Food Regulator Bars Dabur From Selling Products With Misleading '100%' Claims
excerpt: FSSAI issues a prohibition order against Dabur India for labeling products as '100% Natural' and '100% Pure' without valid regulatory backing.
body:
• India's FSSAI issued a prohibition order against Dabur India on Monday, barring the sale of food products labeled as "100% Natural," "100% Pure," or "100% Organic."
  • The order covers honey, apple cider vinegar, coconut oil, cow ghee, coconut water, and coconut milk sold on Dabur's website.
  • FSSAI said some products displayed the "Jaivik Bharat" organic certification logo without valid endorsement from the regulator.
  • Dabur has been given 15 days to submit an Action Taken Report; the company had previously ignored an earlier notice to remove misleading claims.

The Prohibition Order

India's Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI) on Monday issued a prohibition order against Dabur India, barring the company from selling food products that carry misleading "100%" claims on their labels and packaging.

In a social media post, the regulator said products sold on Dabur's website claimed to be "100% Natural," "100% Pure," and "100% Organic" — descriptions the FSSAI called "ambiguous, unverifiable, and likely to mislead consumers."

The prohibition covers several popular product lines, including honey, apple cider vinegar, coconut oil, cow ghee, coconut water, and coconut milk. FSSAI has directed Dabur to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days.

A Long-Running Dispute

Monday's order is the latest escalation in a dispute between the regulator and one of India's largest consumer goods companies. FSSAI had previously issued a notice directing Dabur to discontinue the "100%" claims, but the company did not take corrective action, according to the regulator.

The battle began with Dabur's Real juice line, which carried a "100% fruit juice" label. In April 2025, FSSAI told the Delhi High Court that the claim was impermissible under food safety regulations, arguing that products like the Mixed Fruit variant contained just 6.8% juice concentrate, with the remainder consisting of added water and flavoring agents.

"The term '100%' is not defined or referenced in any manner under the Food Safety Act. Its usage conveys a false sense of absolute purity or superiority and may mislead consumers."

— FSSAI Advisory, 2025

Dabur challenged the directive, arguing it was based on a misinterpretation of existing regulations and that its reconstituted juices — made by adding water to fruit concentrate — comply with FSSAI standards.

Broader Crackdown on Food Labels

The Dabur order is part of a wider FSSAI push to clean up food labeling across the industry. In May 2025, the regulator issued a blanket advisory instructing all food business operators to remove "100%" claims from labels, packaging, and promotional materials. The advisory noted that the term is "not defined or referenced in the Food Safety Act, 2006" and could create "a false impression of absolute purity."

A Scroll investigation earlier this year found that of 163 products flagged by FSSAI for misleading claims — some dating back to 2022 — nearly 120 continued to be sold with the same packaging. Companies named included Dabur, Britannia, Tata 1mg, and Patanjali.

FSSAI also flagged some Dabur products for displaying the "Jaivik Bharat" logo, a certification the regulator introduced to identify organic food. The products carried the logo without valid FSSAI endorsement, according to Monday's order.

What NRI Shoppers Should Know

Dabur products are a staple in Indian grocery stores across the United States, the United Kingdom, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. The company's honey, chyawanprash, and ghee are among its top-selling lines in diaspora markets. While the FSSAI order applies to domestic sales and Dabur's website, label changes required under the ruling could eventually ripple through to exported products.

For NRI consumers who rely on "100% Pure" or "100% Natural" branding as a quality signal, the FSSAI's position is clear: such claims have no regulatory definition in India and should not be treated as verified guarantees of product composition. Under current law, the maximum penalty for non-compliance is ₹10 lakh — a fraction of what major FMCG companies earn from the products in question.
nri_angle: Many NRIs regularly purchase Dabur products abroad, from honey to ghee. This ruling may force label changes on products sold in Indian grocery stores worldwide.
